title: The Case for Slow Reading
focus: Inversion and subordinate clauses of concession
paragraphs: I used to boast that I could finish a novel in an evening. These days I am less proud of it, and not because the novels got worse. Looking back, I realise that most of the books I raced through have left almost nothing behind: a vague mood, the name of a character, perhaps a line or two. The speed that once seemed like a talent now looks more like a way of missing the point.

The habit is not entirely my fault. We have been trained, by years of scrolling and skimming, to extract information quickly and move on. Efficiency is a virtue in many parts of life, and nobody should read a bus timetable slowly. But literature is a different kind of text. It does not exist to deliver facts; it exists to produce an experience, and experiences cannot be accelerated without being altered.

Consider what happens when one reads a sentence by a writer such as Clarice Lispector or Gabriel García Márquez at the pace of a news item. The meaning is understood, but the music is lost. The rhythm of the clauses, the placing of a single adjective, the pause before a verb, all these are invisible to the eye in a hurry. Only by slowing down does one notice that the sentence has been built, word by word, like a small house.

Slow reading is not, however, the same as reading slowly for its own sake. It is a form of attention that includes going back, stopping to wonder why a phrase has been chosen and sometimes closing the book to think. Students who annotate a text in the margins often discover that they understand it better, not because they read more, but because they have been forced to hold each idea in the mind long enough to answer it.

Critics might say that this is a privilege. Who has the time, they ask, to read like a monk? The objection deserves a serious reply. It is true that exhausted people tend to prefer light entertainment, and there is nothing shameful in that. Yet fifteen unhurried minutes a day cost less than a film and often give more. The real obstacle is rarely a shortage of minutes; it is the feeling that unhurried time is wasted time.

There is also a social dimension. A book read slowly invites conversation, since it leaves the reader with something to say. Book clubs flourish for exactly this reason, and so do the neighbourhood libraries that organise them. When a group of strangers agree to read one chapter a week, the conversation that follows is often richer than any online discussion, if only because everyone has had time to think.

None of this means that quick reading should be abolished. We need both speeds, as a driver needs both the motorway and the village street. What we have lost is the second gear. The remedy is humble and almost embarrassingly simple: choose one book you love, put the phone in another room and allow it to take as long as it wishes. You may be surprised by how much of it remains once you have finished.

title: Who Gets to Call a Neighbourhood Authentic?
paragraphs: The first time I heard a stranger describe my neighbourhood as authentic, I was standing in a queue outside a coffee shop in Medellín, waiting for a drink that cost as much as a day's lunch at the corner restaurant. The word was said with admiration, almost with reverence, by a visitor in linen trousers who had been in the city for three days. I smiled politely, and I have been thinking about it ever since.

Authenticity, as the word is used in travel guides and property advertisements, tends to mean the same thing: modest, a little worn, charming to look at. It is a quality that outsiders discover and residents are rarely asked to define. When a street is declared authentic, prices usually follow. The grocery becomes a gallery, the bakery becomes a bistro, and the people who gave the place its character are gradually priced out by their own reputation.

I do not wish to blame the newcomers. Many of them are young professionals who are themselves renting small rooms for more than they can comfortably afford, and who love the city sincerely. Nor is change a crime. Neighbourhoods have always evolved, and a street frozen in time would be a museum rather than a home. What I question is the assumption that change is a natural process, like weather, with nobody in particular responsible for it.

In reality, decisions are involved. Landlords choose to raise rents or to convert flats into short-term lets, which are more profitable than ordinary tenancy agreements. Developers choose which buildings to demolish, and councils decide which permits to grant. It has been argued that lasting protection for existing residents requires rules, such as limits on temporary rentals and incentives for long leases, rather than polite requests for visitors to behave better.

Some residents, to be fair, welcome the transformation. A shopkeeper I know, who has run the same hardware store for thirty years, told me that his sales have never been higher. Others sold family properties at a price that allowed them to retire. These are real benefits, and a column of this kind that ignored them would be dishonest. The difficulty is that the benefits are not shared equally: owners tend to gain, while tenants, who are usually the majority, tend to lose.

Perhaps the most uncomfortable aspect is cultural. When a place becomes valuable because it is authentic, the residents are expected to remain authentic for the benefit of the paying public. They are meant to keep the faded paint, the street music and the old customs, as though they were exhibits. But a community is not a performance. It has the right to renovate, to modernise and to change its mind, without being accused of betraying itself.

So the next time somebody uses the word to praise a place, I would suggest a simple question: authentic according to whom? If the answer comes from those who live there, it deserves our attention. If it comes only from those who are passing through, it may well be a polite way of saying that they have found something to consume.

title: Dumped in the Desert
paragraphs: From the hills above Alto Hospicio, a city in northern Chile, the Atacama Desert looks at first like any other stretch of sand. Then the eye catches a patch of colour, and another, and slowly the slope resolves into garments: jackets, jeans, sports shirts and wedding dresses, in heaps several metres deep. Local people say that the fabric has been arriving for years. Its sheer scale, they add, is difficult to describe to anyone who has not stood beside it.

The clothes reach Chile legitimately. The northern port of Iquique is a free-trade zone, and used garments from Europe, Asia and North America arrive there in bales, bought by importers who resell them throughout the country and beyond. Tens of thousands of tonnes pass through each year. In principle, the trade is useful: it provides cheap clothing and employment. In practice, a large proportion of each bale is of such poor quality that nobody will buy it.

Importers told us that they cannot always predict what a bale contains. They pay by weight, and the bales are sealed before they leave their country of origin. Those who open a bale and find it unsellable have a problem, since legal disposal at an approved facility costs money. One trader, who asked not to be named, said that the temptation to leave the surplus somewhere else was considerable. 'Nobody is watching the desert,' he said.

The result is a series of informal dumps, some of which are on fire. Textile waste does not decompose cleanly. Synthetic fibres release chemicals when burned, and the smoke drifts over the settlements nearby. A local woman, Mariela Cárdenas, who earns a few thousand pesos a day by picking through the piles for wearable items, told us that her children had developed a persistent cough. She does not blame the dumps in particular, but she does not rule them out.

The municipality says that it lacks the resources to clean up the sites. The cost of removing a single dump, an official estimated, would exceed the annual budget for local environmental protection. Meanwhile, national authorities have discussed measures that would make producers responsible for the waste their products eventually create. Such proposals are common in Europe, but they have yet to be applied to clothing in Chile.

Fashion brands, approached for comment, mostly pointed to their recycling initiatives. Few could say how much of their unsold stock ends up in the second-hand market, and none accepted responsibility for the final destination of garments. 'Once we sell it, it is the customer's property,' said one company spokesperson, a statement that is technically true and entirely beside the point.

What happens in Alto Hospicio is not an accident of geography. It follows logically from a system that encourages the constant production of cheap clothing, assumes that somebody else will deal with the consequences and rewards the cheapest solution. Until the real cost of a garment includes its disposal, the desert will continue to fill. It would be comforting to believe that this is a distant problem. The label inside your jacket may say otherwise.

title: Coming Home: The Restitution Debate
paragraphs: Walk through the great museums of London, Paris or Berlin and you will find, in galleries bearing the names of rich donors, objects that were never made for them. A carved door from West Africa, a burial mask from the Andes, sculptures from a temple on a Greek hill. Many were acquired in the nineteenth century, when European powers took what they wished and described the process as rescue. The question of whether such objects should now be returned has become one of the most heated in the world of culture.

The case for restitution is clearest when the circumstances of acquisition were violent. In 1897, a British military expedition entered the city of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, and removed thousands of brass and ivory works, many of which were later sold to museums. Few historians dispute that this was looting. Had the objects been taken today, no museum would dream of displaying them without apology. Why, then, should the passage of time alter the moral calculation?

Defenders of the museums offer several replies. The first is practical: the objects have been preserved, studied and shown to millions of visitors who could not travel to their places of origin. The second is philosophical, and holds that great works belong to humanity as a whole rather than to any single nation. The third is more cautious: if every disputed object were returned, they ask, where would the process end?

Each of these arguments has some force, yet none is entirely convincing. Preservation is a fine achievement, but it hardly entitles anyone to ownership. The idea of universal heritage sounds generous, but it has strangely tended to favour the institutions that already hold the treasures. As for the slippery slope, it overlooks the fact that most claims concern a limited number of objects with a clear history of removal.

What I find more interesting is how the conversation has begun to change. Several museums have agreed to return pieces to their countries of origin, and others have established long-term loans, joint exhibitions or digital archives that give the communities concerned a voice in how their heritage is described. These arrangements are imperfect, but they replace the old question, who owns the object, with a better one: who is responsible for it, and for whom is it held?

The Greek government's long campaign for the return of the sculptures taken from the Parthenon in the early nineteenth century shows the difficulty. The dispute is as much about symbolism as about marble. A nation that has known occupation wants its monument to be whole again; a museum fears that giving way will undermine its collection. Neither motive is contemptible, and a solution will require patience on both sides.

Whatever one's position, the debate has already achieved something valuable. It has forced institutions to ask where their collections came from, a question that was too seldom asked a generation ago. Had it been asked earlier, many of the current controversies might have been avoided. The museums of the future, I suspect, will be judged not only by what they hold, but by how honestly they tell the story of how they came to hold it.
glossary: pendiente resbaladiza (argumento de que un paso lleva a otros)

title: The Fungal Internet Beneath the Forest
focus: Hedging language and complex noun phrases
paragraphs: Under the floor of a temperate forest lies a world that most walkers never consider. A single handful of soil may contain kilometres of thread-like fungal filaments, thinner than a hair and woven among the roots of the trees above. Many of these fungi form a partnership with the trees known as a mycorrhiza: the fungus draws water and minerals from the soil and passes some of them to the tree, in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis.

This partnership is well established and unquestioned. What has stirred controversy is a more dramatic claim. Some popular books and documentaries have described the fungal threads as a kind of forest internet, through which trees share food, send warnings about insects and even support their own offspring. The image is attractive, and it has inspired many people to see forests as cooperative communities rather than collections of competing individuals.

Scientists who work on the subject are more cautious. It is demonstrated that fungal networks can link the roots of different trees, and experiments have shown that small amounts of carbon can move from one tree to another through them. What is far less clear is how often this happens in natural conditions, how much carbon is involved, and whether the receiving tree benefits in a meaningful way. A transfer of a few molecules is not the same as a gift of lunch.

Critics have also questioned the language. Terms such as 'mother trees' or 'communication' suggest intention, and there is no evidence that trees plan to help one another. It may be that the movement of nutrients is simply a by-product of how the fungus manages its own resources, favouring whichever host provides the best return. In this view, the forest is less a family than a marketplace, with all the competition that implies.

Nevertheless, it would be a mistake to dismiss the idea altogether. Research continues to show that fungal networks influence how seedlings establish themselves, how stressed trees survive drought and how carbon is stored in forest soil. A young tree that is connected to a mature network seems, in several studies, to grow more successfully than one that has been isolated. Whether the cause is generosity or opportunism, the practical effect for the seedling may be similar.

The debate has useful consequences for forestry. If fungi matter as much as they appear to, then clear-cutting does more than remove trees; it may damage the underground system on which regrowth depends. Some foresters now leave older trees standing, and take care to disturb the soil as little as possible. These measures are inexpensive, and they would be worth adopting even if the strongest claims about tree cooperation proved exaggerated.

What emerges from all this is a lesson in how science and storytelling interact. A compelling image can draw people to a subject, but it can also run ahead of the evidence. The best response is neither to reject the image nor to adopt it uncritically, but to keep asking what we actually know. The forest floor is still far more mysterious than any metaphor suggests.
glossary: huésped, organismo que acoge a otro

title: The Seed Banker
paragraphs: The refrigerated room where Mariam Haddad works is kept at a temperature few people would choose to spend a day in. Shelves of small glass jars stretch back into the cold, each containing seeds of a particular variety of maize, bean or quinoa. To a visitor, they look like spices. To Haddad, a Chilean agronomist of Palestinian descent, they are an insurance policy against a future in which today's farmers lose the crops they depend on.

Haddad, fifty-two, directs a regional seed bank in central Chile, one of more than a thousand such facilities worldwide. Their purpose is to store the genetic diversity of cultivated plants, including old local varieties that farmers have abandoned in favour of higher-yielding ones. 'A variety may seem unimportant,' she says, 'until a disease arrives and it turns out to be the only one that resists it.' Such resistance, once lost, cannot easily be recreated.

The best-known facility of this kind is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, in Norway, which opened in 2008 and stores duplicates of samples held by banks around the world. Haddad's bank has deposited copies there, in line with a system in which each country keeps its own collection and sends a backup to the Arctic. 'It is like a safe-deposit box,' she explains. 'We remain the owners of what is inside.'

The work is less glamorous than it sounds. Seeds must be dried to a precise level of moisture, tested regularly to check that they can still germinate, and periodically regrown so that fresh seed can replace old. Haddad's team includes technicians who spend entire weeks in greenhouses, counting seedlings. 'Nobody writes songs about germination rates,' she says, with a dry smile, 'but they are the whole business.'

Her most rewarding projects involve people rather than jars. A few years ago, a farming community in the south asked for help after a flood destroyed their stored seed. Haddad's team found, among the bank's samples, a potato variety that had been collected from the same valley decades earlier, and returned it to the villagers. 'They cried,' she recalls. 'Not because of the potato itself, but because they had not known that anyone was looking after it.'

The bank is financed mainly by government grants, which Haddad regards as both a blessing and a risk. Budgets change, and priorities with them. She has therefore begun to build partnerships with universities and farming cooperatives, so that the seeds are used and not merely stored. 'A collection nobody asks for is a museum,' she says, 'and museums are the first things to be cut.'

Asked whether she is optimistic, Haddad hesitates. The threats to crop diversity are real, from climate change to the spread of a handful of commercial varieties across the world. Yet each time a farmer plants a rescued seed, she says, the argument is won a little. 'We do not preserve the past,' she tells me, closing the cold-room door. 'We keep the future from having fewer options.'

title: Salt
topic: Work, inheritance and the Bolivian highlands
focus: Narrative tenses, inversion and participle clauses
paragraphs: At dawn, the salt flat looked like a second sky. The water that had gathered overnight in its shallow hollows reflected the clouds so perfectly that Rosa could not tell, from the edge of the village, where the ground ended. Her father used to say that Uyuni was the only place where a person could walk on the sky without being punished for it. She had been nine when he first said it. She was thirty now, and she no longer found it funny.

Don Eusebio had worked the salt for forty years. Each morning he cut the crust into blocks, piled the heaps with a shovel and loaded them on a truck, earning, in a good week, a few hundred bolivianos. He never complained, and he never expected his daughter to follow him. When she left for La Paz to study chemistry, he drove her to the bus station, shook her hand like a stranger and gave her a small bag of salt for luck.

She returned only twice in twelve years, both times for funerals. This was the third occasion, and the funeral was his. The village had changed less than she expected. There were more hostels for tourists and a new museum made of salt bricks, but the old men still sat outside the shop with their hats pulled low. One of them, who had worked alongside her father, held her hand a moment too long.

'He talked about you,' he said. 'Not to you, perhaps. But to us.' He described how Don Eusebio had carried her university results in his pocket for a whole year, showing them to anybody who would look. He had pretended not to understand a word, but he had learned the name of every course. 'Organic chemistry,' the old man said, pronouncing it with pride, as one might carry something fragile. 'He could say it better than I can.'

Rosa had not cried at the service. She did not cry now either, but something in her chest shifted, like a heavy object that has been moved an inch. She walked out onto the flat in the afternoon, under a sky so blue it hurt, and knelt to taste the crust. It was exactly as she remembered: sharp, clean and unmistakably honest.

The company where she worked in La Paz paid her well to test the purity of industrial minerals. She had always felt, with a mild guilt, that the job was a distant cousin of her father's. Now she understood that the distance had been in her mind. The same hands that tested a sample under a microscope had once, long ago, learned from his hands how to judge the grain of salt by its sound.

She stayed until the end of the week. On the last evening, she borrowed a shovel and worked beside the others for an hour, clumsily, to the quiet amusement of the men. At dusk, the pools filled again with sky. This time, Rosa stepped into one of them, shoes and all, and did not feel in the least that she was being punished.

questions.q: Rosa cried at her father's funeral service.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'Rosa had not cried at the service'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Don Eusebio's feelings for his daughter?
options: He did not understand her studies at all
He was angry that she had left the village
He was proud of her, though he rarely showed it
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: la despidió con un apretón de manos formal, pero aprendió el nombre de cada curso y mostraba sus notas con orgullo.

questions.q: What is the mood at the end of the story?
options: Excited and playful
Peaceful and reconciled
Bitter and regretful
questions.explain_es: Tono: Rosa trabaja junto a los demás y entra en el agua sin sentirse castigada; el final transmite reconciliación serena.

questions.q: Why does the author describe the salt flat as 'a second sky' in the opening?
options: To show that Rosa dislikes the place
To introduce an image that returns at the end
To explain why the village is poor
questions.explain_es: Propósito/estructura: la imagen del cielo y del castigo del primer párrafo reaparece al final, cuando el agua se llena de cielo y Rosa ya no se siente castigada.

questions.q: What does Rosa realise about her job in the sixth paragraph?
options: It is related to her father's work
It has nothing to do with salt
It is much better than his work
questions.explain_es: Comprende que su trabajo era 'a distant cousin' del de su padre; la distancia 'had been in her mind'.

questions.q: In 'something in her chest shifted', the author means that she…
options: moved away from the place
felt an emotional change
had a physical illness
questions.explain_es: Es una expresión figurada: sintió un cambio emocional sin llegar a llorar.

title: Public Library Usage Review
focus: Formal report language and data comparison
paragraphs: ## 1. Introduction

This review examines how the public library network of a medium-sized Colombian city of approximately 400,000 inhabitants was used over the past three years. It draws on loan records, door counts, a survey of 900 users and interviews with fourteen members of staff. The objective is to establish whether the network is meeting the needs of the population it serves, and to identify areas in which resources might be better directed.
## 2. Findings on use

Book loans fell by 23 per cent over the period, continuing a decline that began before the review. During the same time, visits rose by 17 per cent, and attendance at free workshops, which include coding for teenagers and Spanish classes for newly arrived families, doubled. In short, fewer people come to borrow books, but more come to use the building.

The pattern varies by branch. The two central libraries record the lowest growth in visits and the highest decline in loans, whereas the three neighbourhood branches in the south of the city show the strongest rise in attendance. Staff at those branches report that users, many of them young adults, stay for several hours to study or to use the free internet connection.
## 3. User views

Satisfaction was high overall, with 84 per cent of respondents rating the service as good or very good. The most common complaints concerned opening hours, with 41 per cent of users saying that they would use the library more if it opened on Sunday afternoons. Only 6 per cent mentioned the quality of the book collection as a concern, although respondents were more critical of the availability of recent titles.

Interviews with staff add a further dimension. Librarians described spending a growing share of their time helping users with tasks that are not strictly related to books, such as filling in online forms for public benefits, applying for jobs or printing documents for official procedures. Several said that they had received no formal training for this work, although all considered it a valuable part of the service.
## 4. Resources

The annual budget, currently around two billion pesos, has not risen in real terms since the start of the period. Approximately 70 per cent is spent on salaries and maintenance, leaving a limited amount for new acquisitions and programmes. Several managers noted that the cost of replacing outdated computers is not included in the regular budget, which obliges them to seek external funds.

A comparison with the previous review, carried out five years earlier, shows that the proportion of users under thirty has risen from 31 per cent to 46 per cent. Over the same period, the proportion of users over sixty has fallen slightly. The reviewers note that this shift is likely to continue, and that service planning should therefore anticipate demand for study space, reliable internet access and extended evening hours.
## 5. Recommendations

It is recommended that the network extend its opening hours at the three neighbourhood branches on a trial basis, using volunteers where possible. It is also recommended that the council establish a modest fund for replacing equipment, and that future evaluations record the number of hours spent in the building, rather than visits alone. A measure based only on loans, the review argues, no longer reflects what libraries actually do.
glossary: conteo de visitantes en la puerta

questions.q: The review found that book loans fell while visits to the libraries increased.
questions.explain_es: Los préstamos bajaron un 23 por ciento y las visitas subieron un 17 por ciento.

questions.q: Most respondents were dissatisfied with the service overall.
questions.explain_es: El 84 por ciento valoró el servicio como bueno o muy bueno.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the growth in workshop attendance?
options: Workshops are gradually replacing the book collections
Libraries are being used for more than borrowing books
People no longer want to read any books at all
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: 'fewer people come to borrow books, but more come to use the building'; la biblioteca cumple otras funciones.

questions.q: How does the report treat the opening-hours complaint?
options: As the main concern, deserving a trial response
As a minor issue affecting few users
As an unfair criticism to be ignored
questions.explain_es: Tono/actitud: es la queja más común (41 por ciento) y la recomendación principal propone ampliar horarios de forma experimental.

questions.q: Why does the report recommend recording hours in the building?
options: Because staff want to reduce their workload
Because loans alone no longer reflect real use
Because the council requires more statistics
questions.explain_es: Propósito: se argumenta que una medida basada solo en préstamos 'no longer reflects what libraries actually do'.

questions.q: How is the review organised?
options: Questions followed by brief answers from experts
A diary of events written month by month by staff
Introduction, findings, views, resources, recommendations
questions.explain_es: Estructura: las secciones siguen el orden típico de un informe: introducción, hallazgos, opiniones, recursos y recomendaciones.

questions.q: In 'continuing a decline', 'decline' means…
options: a gradual fall
a polite refusal
a sudden rise
questions.explain_es: 'Decline' es una disminución gradual.

title: Nostalgia as a Political Tool
paragraphs: Almost everyone feels nostalgia, and most of us feel it harmlessly. A song from adolescence, the smell of a grandmother's kitchen, the sound of a school bell: such things can produce a pleasant ache that few would wish to be without. It is therefore easy to see why politicians are drawn to the emotion. A feeling that is so widely shared, so warm and so impossible to contradict is a rare gift for anyone who wants to be believed.

The typical formula is simple. First, a golden age is described, a time when streets were safe, families were united and the nation was respected. Second, the present is shown to be a falling-off from that age. Third, someone is identified as responsible, often a foreign power, a minority or the elite. The final step is the promise to restore the past. Slogans that promise to make a country great again follow this pattern, and they exist in many languages.

What makes the technique effective is that it needs no evidence. Memory is selective, and nostalgia is more selective still. People remember the sunny holidays and forget the shortages, the fear and the quiet injustices that accompanied them. A historian who tries to complicate the picture is likely to be told that she is attacking the good old days, and therefore, by implication, the people who lived through them.

It would be unfair, however, to claim that nostalgia is always manipulative. Some of it is a legitimate response to loss. A town that has seen its factory close and its young people leave may reasonably look back with longing, and it is hardly surprising that residents feel ignored by those who talk only about the future. Politicians who dismiss such feelings as irrational are making a mistake of their own, one that is easily exploited by their opponents.

The distinction that matters, I think, lies between nostalgia that looks backward in order to grieve and nostalgia that looks backward in order to blame. The first accepts that the past is gone and seeks a way to honour it. The second insists that the past was stolen, and that it can be recovered by punishing somebody. The first leads to memorials, festivals and sometimes to better planning. The second tends to lead to resentment.

Is there a defence against this rhetoric? A partial one, at least, is curiosity. When someone invokes a golden age, we can ask which year they mean, and for whom it was golden. Such questions are not hostile. They simply insist on specifics, and nostalgia, like most comforting stories, does not survive well in the presence of specifics. The women, the migrants and the poor of any supposed golden age usually remember it differently.

None of this means that we should banish the past from politics, even if we could. Societies need memory, and they need affection for their own history. What they do not need is a past invented for the purposes of the present. The most useful kind of loyalty to the past is accuracy: remembering it as it was, with its beauty and its injustice, and refusing to let it be used as a weapon.
glossary: hacer el duelo, llorar una pérdida

questions.q: The author claims that all nostalgia is manipulative.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'It would be unfair, however, to claim that nostalgia is always manipulative'; puede ser una respuesta legítima a una pérdida.

questions.q: The author suggests that asking for specifics weakens nostalgic rhetoric.
questions.explain_es: Afirma que la nostalgia 'does not survive well in the presence of specifics'.

questions.q: What does the author imply about the people who do not remember the golden age fondly?
options: They are usually mistaken about what the past was like
They are the people who invented the political slogans
Their experience is often left out of nostalgic stories
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: mujeres, migrantes y pobres 'usually remember it differently'; la narrativa nostálgica suele omitir su experiencia.

questions.q: How would you describe the author's overall tone?
options: Sentimental and uncritical
Analytical and balanced
Mocking and dismissive
questions.explain_es: Tono: analiza la técnica, reconoce la nostalgia legítima y propone distinguir sus usos, sin burlarse.

questions.q: Why does the author distinguish between grieving and blaming nostalgia?
options: To separate a healthy use from a harmful one
To prove that all politicians are the same
To argue that nostalgia should be banned
questions.explain_es: Propósito: la distinción permite separar la nostalgia que honra el pasado de la que culpa a alguien y genera resentimiento.

questions.q: What is the function of the second paragraph?
options: It outlines a typical pattern of nostalgic rhetoric
It tells a personal childhood story
It rejects the argument of the first paragraph
questions.explain_es: Estructura: describe en cuatro pasos la fórmula típica: edad de oro, decadencia, culpable y promesa de restaurar.

questions.q: In 'a historian who tries to complicate the picture', 'complicate' means…
options: make it more beautiful
make it more famous
make it less simple
questions.explain_es: 'Complicate the picture' es hacer la imagen menos simple, añadiendo matices.
